title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, an aggregated difficulty summary drawn from the archived task manifest, a diagnostic analysis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings while verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes?

Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator; and (3) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reuse of a single deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run, together with concrete benchmark‑hardening recommendations.
sections.related_work:
This study draws from three strands. First, intent→configuration generation: recent work demonstrates LLMs can synthesize usable configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds (e.g., Nguyen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024) but most evaluations emphasize generation quality rather than staged rollout safety. Second, verifier‑guided and generate–validate–repair workflows report correctness gains in IaC and provisioning contexts (e.g., Jana et al., 2026), motivating runtime guard integrations but without production‑scale closed‑loop proofs. Third, deterministic network verification and reachability tools (header‑space style, Kubernetes reachability) are effective at finding configuration errors offline (e.g., Liu et al., 2025) and suggest a role for runtime blocking. Surveys highlight an evaluation gap: action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited. Our work operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility and to surface practical design pitfalls.

Key verified references used for positioning are listed in References.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% confidence intervals (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes.

Adapter semantics and shared generation. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer. Critically, preregistration set shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false): each task provoked a single deterministic LLM generation delivered identically to both baseline and guarded episodes. This isolates validator acceptance on identical outputs rather than exposing generator variance.

Episode flow, validator policy, and repair rules. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate to both episodes, and (in the guarded episode) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation. A single repair attempt per guarded episode was permitted by design; repair_applied flags and validator_trace states were recorded. In this run repair_applied = false across episodes.

Task generation and deterministic replay. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and annotated with difficulty metadata (level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; reproducible simulator failure or nondeterminism would lead to exclusion. All three‑replay checks passed in this run.
sections.results:
Execution summary and reconciliation. Run start: 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z; completion: 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). Baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0). Guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Preregistered permutation test p = 1.0; exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen’s h = 0.0. These values are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Repairs and rollbacks. Across 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations, explaining universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes.

Aggregated task difficulty summary. We computed per‑task difficulty counts directly from the archived task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Aggregated counts and percentages: medium = 120 tasks (30.0%), hard = 160 tasks (40.0%), very_hard = 120 tasks (30.0%). (See caption and artifact reference below for the manifest path and hash.)

Statistical interpretation. The observed deterministic ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but these statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply.
sections.discussion:
Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings.

Implications for design and power. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair differences; the lack of variance collapsed statistical power and rendered confirmatory inference about guard utility moot in this run. Correctly diagnosing this failure mode requires artifact grounding: validator_trace records, per‑task validation_before/after snapshots, and the shared response payloads in execution/responses/* together show the shared candidate accepted in every pair.

Artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations. Derived directly from archived traces and task metadata we recommend: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs; (2) use distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorers (or a held‑out scorer) to avoid conflating runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; (3) preregister controlled perturbation seeds that produce reproducible baseline failure rates to preserve signal; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling to guarantee a minimum fraction of very_hard tasks; and (5) instrument repair attempts and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes. The archived manifest and validator_trace entries already contain the fields required to implement these changes reproducibly.

Operational lessons. For practitioners: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide potential benefits of runtime guards; (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important to measure guard impact; and (iii) benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve generator variance or include adversarial perturbations.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete steps researchers can preregister to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings.

Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata (execution/task_manifest.jsonl), and the analysis results (paired contingency and bootstrap outputs). Auditors can reproduce reported summaries from these artifacts.

Final interpretive boundary. The null paired difference observed here is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design. It should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general but as an example of how specific preregistered design choices can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate generator×guard closed‑loop effects.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be audited; Table 3 reports the aggregated counts computed from that manifest.
